nonblocking.claim_broken: T1 / the mutant invariant 'the destination is exactly the scheme + the handle' and 'the issued handle is upl_ + 22..64 url-safe characters'. The equality check and the fullmatch are only partly proved.
nonblocking.evidence: Two reviewer single-edit mutants survived (1 passed). (a) `ticket["destination_ref"] != UPLOAD_SCHEME + handle` -> `not ticket["destination_ref"].startswith(UPLOAD_SCHEME)`: a store that issues `infrx-upload:<org>/<handle>` would render the org. (b) `UPLOAD_HANDLE_RE.fullmatch(handle)` -> `.match(handle)`: a valid handle with a suffix would render. The two rewrites in the case (an s3:// key and `upl_x`) cannot tell these apart. The declared mutants, endswith/`in`-style weakenings, a wrong scheme constant and a startswith('upl_') handle check all die. The code is correct as written, M3's real store is correct, and T1 was nonblocking in round 1.
nonblocking.minimal_fix: Add two rewrites to the same case: destination_ref = f"infrx-upload:{org}/{handle}" (scheme kept, value wrong), and upload_handle = valid_handle + "/x" with destination_ref = "infrx-upload:" + that handle. Expect 500 and assert neither value appears in the body.

The refusal case asserts only 403, 404 and 400. The 504s already get close from intake's CLOSE_CODES. A 500 (for example the T1 ticket refusal) or a pre-read 5xx such as an auth-backend failure in tenant() would lose the header unnoticed. The claimed pre-read 4xx refusals (the round-1 T3 scope) are fully proved: the declared mutant, `in (403, 404)` and `>= 500` all die at the close assertion.

nonblocking.claim_broken: T1: the issued handle must fullmatch UPLOAD_HANDLE_RE. Weakening fullmatch to match is not killed.
nonblocking.evidence: Reviewer mutant handle_match_not_fullmatch SURVIVED: 26 passed. Concrete input: handle = "upl_" + 43*"A" + "/1a1a1a1a-0000-4000-8000-000000000001" gives match True and fullmatch False. A store issuing that handle, with a destination_ref that agrees with it, would be rendered with the org in both fields. The equality check does not catch it because both sides carry the same suffix. The test's only bad handle is `upl_x`, which neither match nor fullmatch accepts.
nonblocking.minimal_fix: Add a rewrite whose handle is a valid handle plus a suffix (for example "/" + org), with destination_ref = "infrx-upload:" + that handle. Expect 500, with the org absent.

nonblocking.claim_broken: The docstring says the upload pool 'must be the pool the chat ingress uses, so both share the bound'. The fallback chain meets this only when a composition root sets rt.large_bodies or IngressDeps.large_bodies. IngressDeps.large_bodies defaults to None, and in that case Ingress mints its own pool (ingress.py:119, `self.slots`), which is not reachable from rt, and uploads mints a second one.
nonblocking.evidence: Probe: rt.ingress = support.deps() (large_bodies None), then ingress.register and uploads.register on one app. The ingress pool is not the uploads pool: `ing.slots is up_slots` is False, with limit 2 each, so one process allows 4 concurrent large bodies. This is residual from round 1, not a regression. The round-2 claim ('else a new pool') describes it honestly. The pool is also fixed at mount: setting rt.large_bodies after register is not consulted (PUT 204 with the late pool full), so two requests can never pick different pools. The reviewer mutant ingress_before_runtime_pool (swapping the order of rt.large_bodies and rt.ingress.large_bodies) survives, but it is observable only when both are set to different pools, which is itself a misconfiguration.
nonblocking.minimal_fix: Coordinator composition: set one LargeBodies on both rt.large_bodies and IngressDeps.large_bodies when adding uploads to ROUTERS. Optionally, in pilot mode, have uploads.register raise RuntimeMisconfigured when neither is set, instead of minting.

nonblocking.claim_broken: Connection: close applies to refusals only. Nothing pins that a 201, 204 or 200 keeps the connection.
nonblocking.evidence: Reviewer mutant close_on_success_too (`>= 400` changed to `>= 200`) SURVIVED: 26 passed. Measured on the real code: 201, 204 and 200 carry no Connection header (correct). Every refusal from 400 to 500 carries close. The cost of the mutant would be performance (no keep-alive on success), not correctness.
nonblocking.minimal_fix: In test_media_sec__every_refusal_closes_the_connection, also assert that the create 201 it already makes has headers.get("connection") != "close".

nonblocking.claim_broken: R3: 'the store gets the same deadline'. It gets a second deadline of the same length, not what remains of the first. A large PUT can hold the shared slot for up to about 2 × intake_timeout_s: a read just under the deadline, then a store call just under it.
nonblocking.evidence: Code reading: read_body's deadline and asyncio.wait_for(..., limits.intake_timeout_s) run one after the other. The deadline is still bounded, and a hung store is cut (reviewer mutants store_deadline_x10, store_timeout_not_caught and store_timeout_is_internal were all KILLED). Behaviour on timeout is correct. If the store writes and then hangs, the answer is 504, a retry with the same bytes is 204, a retry with other bytes is 409 (correct write-once), and complete is 200. No upload is left stuck, and in_flight is 0. Client cancellation during the store call propagates as CancelledError (not a 504), and the slot is released. A TimeoutError raised by the store itself maps to 504 with no leak.
nonblocking.minimal_fix: Either word the claim as 'a further intake_timeout_s', or pass the remaining budget (deadline minus elapsed on a monotonic clock) to wait_for.
